The Pentagon is "increasing [nuclear] options available to the President for
purposes of deterring or responding effectively to a nuclear contingency,"
undersecretary of war Elbridge Colby says.

Unless you're a member of the nuclear priesthood, this is probably the first
you're hearing about it. The Senate knows, having been briefed earlier this
month in a [closed hearing](https://www.armed-services.senate.gov/hearings/to-
receive-a-briefing-on-the-implementation-of-the-national-defense-strategy-and-
its-impact-on-global-defense-posture). But neither Congress nor the media have
said a word about the disclosure I quoted (which this humble newsletter is
providing you in its entirety below).

Colby has been making this case for a long time. In 2011, fresh off a Pentagon
stint working on Obama's New START treaty, he wrote about what he thought
America's nuclear war plans should be able to do.

"The United States should maintain the assured ability to conduct a
devastating, effectively annihilating strike against any opponent _even_
_after_ an attempt by that opponent to disarm the United States through a
first strike of its own," Colby
[said](https://www.newparadigmsforum.com/p810). The forces held back for
retaliation, he added, should be able to "destroy the attacking country as a
functioning society."

Sounds like he's got World Wars III-IV covered.

But the same post went on to argue for what he wants now: a limited nuclear
strike capability. The thinking is that this provides the president a
goldilocks-style intermediate option, between the too-cold porridge of doing
nothing and the too-hot porridge of, well, Armageddon.

Here's how we got here. In April, Robert Kadlec, the assistant secretary of
war for nuclear deterrence, [told Congress](https://www.armed-
services.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/04-20-2026_stratforcesub.pdf) that the U.S.
now has to deter Russia and China at the same time, plus a growing roster of
regional nuclear threats. Think: Iran.

Kadlec's wishlist included a nuclear sea-launched cruise missile, which the
first Bush administration eliminated and the Navy doesn't even want. He also
said the U.S. needs new tools to counter nuclear blackmail.

A month later, Colby spelled out the thinking. "We once again find ourselves
grappling with major power rivalry under the nuclear shadow," he
[told](https://www.globalsecurity.org/military/library/news/2026/05/mil-260519-dod02.htm)
senior military officers at the National War College. The defining challenge
of our era, he said, is "how to defend important -- indeed potentially very
important -- but nevertheless not existential interests against nuclear-armed
major powers."

Translation: how to fight Russia or China over something short of national
survival, like an ally's territory.

None of this is hypothetical, not for an administration that went to war with
Iran this year for the stated reason of keeping Tehran from ever getting a
nuclear weapon. In this environment, handing Trump more nuclear options isn't
some wonky policy tweak. This is a question of national survival.

That's not to say that nuclear war is imminent or even likely. But isn't
nuclear policy the kind of thing the public should have some or literally
_any_ say in? Washington of course has zero interest in that. But why does the
news media? It's baffling that they haven't done a single story on this.
Meanwhile, there's wall-to-wall coverage of the hack of FBI data and its
supposed threat to Bureau personnel. That's of interest to the FBI, but why
would any ordinary person give a shit? (The FBI can sign up for the $45 class
action settlement like the rest of us!)

Now compare those headlines with what Colby told the National War College,
foreshadowing what Trump's new nuclear options will mean:

> "I want to underline that the centrality of the political object[ive] does
> not mean simply a brake on military force. To the contrary, in some
> circumstances it may require aggressiveness and an acceptance of great
> risk."

A bit more alarming than some cyber hack, no?

Here's where we're heading:

  * Even lower yield and flexible bomber and aircraft-carried nuclear bombs and air-to-surface missiles to provide more options to Donald Trump in Europe and on the Korean Peninsula.

  * A sea-launched nuclear weapon, so the U.S. can go nuclear without asking allies for permission or for help

  * "[Credible, rational nuclear options](https://www.war.gov/News/Transcripts/Transcript/Article/4567089/remarks-by-under-secretary-of-war-for-policy-elbridge-colby-at-the-2026-united/)," as if "rational" and "nuclear" belong in the same sentence, including limited strikes a president could "plausibly authorize."

Senator Jack Reed, the ranking Democrat on the Armed Services Committee, has
been briefed on everything I've told you in this story and more. It's not
clear why he hasn't said anything. Perhaps the 76-year-old was busy with his
reelection campaign?

Speaking of which, guess who Pete Hegseth just announced would lead his creepy
new Project Meridian future-of-warfare study? 83-year-old Newt Gingrich!

From Cold War-era nuclear brinksmanship to Newt Gingrich, talk about a blast
from the past.
